newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerians vote in peaceful referendum.
newsitem.headline: Algerians vote in peaceful referendum.

text.p: Algerians flooded polling stations on Thursday to vote on a draft constitution that would ban Islamic political parties while state media said threats of violence by Moslem militants did not materialise.
First official figures showed Algerians turning out overwhelmingly to vote, in defiance of the threats and main opposition leaders' calls for a boycott.
Polls closed at 8 p.m. (1900) but by early evening nearly three-quarters of Algeria's 16.4 million eligible voters had cast ballots, Algerian state-run radio said, quoting the interior ministry.

Residents in the garrison town of Blida, 50 km (30 miles) south of Algiers, said the army shelled mountains neary the city on Wednesday night, apparently trying to pre-empt any buildup of Moslem guerrillas. Blida is a route for Moslem guerrillas seeking to carry out attacks around Algiers.
The constitution would ban Moslem militants from gaining power and guerrillas threatened before the plebiscite that they would kill anyone voting.
The national turnout was 71.94 percent at about 6 p.m (1700 GMT), compared to 65.82 percent in last year's presidential election at the same time, official figures showed.
President Liamine Zeroual's government hopes for a large turnout to bolster popularity.
However, Algerian radio said turnout was only at nearly 22 percent in two northeastern Berber provinces where a Berber-dominated party had called for a boycott.
The draft constitution, which states that Arabic language is the sole state language, angered Berber activists who want recognition of their language as an official language as well.
Residents said they saw many "Yes" ballots thrown away near polling stations in Algiers, apparently by voters opposed to the proposed constitution.
Algiers-based diplomats said the government deployed more than 300,000 soldiers and policemen to guard voters across the country, five times the size of France.
Police and paramilitary forces were seen patrolling Algiers streets under drizzling rain and soldiers in combat gear manned roadblocks on main roads outside the city, witnesses said.
More than 60,000 people have died in Algeria's violence since 1992 when the authorities annulled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a huge lead.
The Armed Islamic Group or GIA -- most feared of the country's Moslem guerrilla movements -- warned people not to vote, threatening to slit the throats of anyone who leaves home on referendum day.
President Liamine Zeroual, who cast his ballot at Ghazali school polling station near the presidential palace in Algiers, vowed to respect voters' decision on his proposed reforms.
"The Algerian people is sovereign. Its will would be respected," a smiling Zeroual told reporters after he voted amid tight security.
Zeroual, a former army general, is hoping to match the 75 percent turnout reported in the election that endorsed him in office in last year.
But diplomats said that hopes for change, which flowered last year, withered when violence continued and people felt the hardship of economic reforms required by overseas creditors.
"A year after the presidential election, political deadlock is still total," secular opposition leader Said Saadi said on Wednesday. "Social poverty is worsening every day."

"Even before the results of the referendum are known, the conclusions on the future of democracy are far from being optimistic," said Algerian Liberte newspaper in a comment blasting the government for its tight control on the media.
